name: Mathematicians vs the labs
frame: Working mathematicians pushing back on AI labs’ benchmark claims, while the labs keep posting competition results.
question: Does the dispute change how labs report mathematical results, or how mathematicians engage with them? Settled by: a lab adopting the declaration’s write-up norms, a joint statement, or the Mathathon proceeding without lab sponsorship.

text: As of 14 September the two sides are talking past each other. Twenty-five Fields Medallists signed a declaration, published on Terence Tao's blog on 11 September, that AI labs' benchmark chasing is "severely misaligned" with mathematics; OpenAI pulled its $10,000-per-team sponsorship of Caltech's Mathathon after an open letter from Caltech mathematicians. The same week, an NVIDIA team reported an open Nemotron pipeline scoring 30 of 42 at IMO 2026 with no formal prover or tools, and the Magenta pipeline reported 100% on AIME 2025, AIME 2026 and HMMT February 2026 with Lean-checked proofs.

As of 21 September the mathematicians have started building rather than only objecting. Terence Tao wrote that he co-founded the Foundation for Science and AI Research with private donors to support responsible uses of AI in mathematics and the other sciences, "independent of the major AI companies", and that the foundation is announcing an Open Math Model initiative with open licensed weights and code, published training methods, reproducible evaluations, documented training-data sources and releases that report failures and limitations alongside successes. The announcement says the planned gradual rollout was brought forward: "given current events and the high demand for open models, we are accelerating our schedule". No partners, compute commitments or model sizes are named, and the foundation is collecting expressions of interest.

The measurement of AI use in the field moved at the same time. Epoch AI, in an analysis updated on September 18, reports that the share of mathematics preprints on arXiv acknowledging AI rose from 4% in April to 25% in August, and that in August 6% of all papers explicitly acknowledged that AI made a substantial research contribution. Restricting to papers with at least one author who published regularly before 2023 keeps the acknowledgment rate within 1.5 percentage points of the overall figure each month. Epoch says it analysed every mathematics arXiv preprint from January 2025 to August 2026, classifying acknowledgments with one frontier model and validating with another; a human review of 200 random acknowledgments classified as substantial research or research assistance showed 93% agreement. The measure depends on voluntary disclosure. No lab has adopted the declaration's write-up norms, and the Mathathon's sponsorship remains unresolved in the record.
states.changed: The dispute produced its first institution: Tao's SAIR foundation announced an accelerated open-weight model initiative for mathematics explicitly independent of the labs, while Epoch AI put a number on how fast disclosed AI use is spreading through mathematics preprints.

text: As of 28 September one lab claim has been checked by a named outside expert and the rest have not. Anthropic published a guest post reporting that Claude computed the six-particle hexagon amplitude in planar N=4 super Yang-Mills at nine loops, past the eight-loop record, by two independent routes. Lance Dixon of SLAC and Stanford, who set the eight-loop record, validated it; the disclosure states that he validated the result independently and received Claude usage credits, and that Anthropic invited and compensated the author. The author's own conclusion is that the model did something humans turned out to be able to do as well, using known methods with more compute than people had tried, and the post reports that a group led by Song He at the Chinese Academy of Sciences obtained the majority of the same result concurrently with GPT-6 assistance. Nothing is peer reviewed and the human teams have yet to publish.

On the labs' side of the dispute the reporting norms moved slightly. OpenAI announced an Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study, with nine unpaid initial members who control their own membership and may go public with their views, and said in the same announcement that an internal model has resolved more than 100 additional open problems across most areas of mathematics. No independent verification of that count is reported, the problems are not listed, and the blog post states that the group will not be responsible for advising the company on how to pace its internal progress on mathematics. Only one member of the group signed the open letter that 25 Fields Medallists signed earlier in September. The Mathathon's sponsorship remains unresolved in the record and no lab has adopted the declaration's write-up norms.
states.changed: The first lab claim in this arc was validated by a named outside expert rather than asserted — Lance Dixon checked the nine-loop amplitude — while OpenAI created an advisory group of mathematicians at the same time as claiming a further hundred solved problems that nobody outside the company has verified. The group's own charter excludes advising on pace.

text: As of this week the mathematicians have written the rules they want the labs to follow, and the Mathathon they objected to is going ahead without lab money. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence published "Responsible Release of AI-Generated Mathematics" in late September, drawing on over 600 community replies. Its central rule is that "If AI labs produce significant mathematical results, they should responsibly release the results, as outlined in this document, as soon as possible", paired with the obligation that "AI labs that release substantial mathematical output without immediate accompanying human understanding must take responsibility for ensuring that human understanding will follow". On benchmarking against proprietary models the document states: "we do not endorse this practice, and we ask them to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models."

The Mathathon question this storyline tracked has been answered. A joint statement published by the original student organisers, the open-letter coauthors and other members of the Caltech community set the redesigned event for 13 to 15 November 2026 under the theme "Old Problems, New Proofs", co-organised with the Foundation for Science and AI Research and with XTX Markets as lead donor. Proprietary models are permitted but open-source tools encouraged, and full disclosure and justification of model usage is required, with an explainer and a repository per submission.

On the labs' side the claims kept coming and the verification arrangements did not change. Meta published six mathematics papers written with its own model and said five of them answer previously open research questions, marking which passages were drafted by researchers and which by the model, and acknowledging a separate AI agent that reported a different counterexample to the same conjecture weeks earlier. Anthropic published a guest post describing manuscripts across many fields produced with Claude. Nothing is peer reviewed, no lab has published an adoption statement for the advisory group's norms, and the group's own framing is that it is still advising one lab on how to coordinate the release of results it has claimed.
states.changed: The dispute produced a written standard: the advisory group published release rules for AI-generated mathematics drawing on over 600 replies, and asked the labs to stop benchmarking advanced problems on proprietary models. The Mathathon question is settled — the event is set for November with XTX Markets as lead donor and no lab sponsorship — while Meta added a fresh set of claimed open-problem results that nobody outside the company has checked.

text: As of 12 October the catalogue has its first retractions and the discipline has its first call for non-cooperation. OpenAI's revision log entry of October 7 withdrew three manuscripts, stating that in one "a sign error invalidates a stabilization-trace cancellation argument and the construction used by two dependent papers". The same entry revised 14 others "with proof repairs, corrected statements, clearer hypotheses and dependencies", updated 13 more to cite revised companion papers, and recorded that "This brings the total percentage of top-line results formalized to 300 / 719 = ~42%." The README now reads "The current catalogue contains 719 manuscripts organized into 372 families", where the release was reported as 722. An OpenAI spokesperson told Retraction Watch: "Where errors are identified, we will work to correct them promptly and withdraw papers if no fixes can be found." Cornell's Alex Townsend told Retraction Watch he suspects more errors will be found, and said the Lean-verified manuscripts ought to have been announced first. The log has no entry dated later in the week.

The Association for Human Mathematics Communications Working Group, in a statement dated October 7 reposted as a guest post on Terence Tao's blog, wrote that "Mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done" and that "Releasing over 700 files at once is not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power. We urge mathematicians to discontinue their work with OpenAI and to return to a vision of science that centers human understanding." It named "The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, from whom OpenAI has claimed to derive its legitimacy", and noted that OpenAI "is currently defending lawsuits against accusations of illegal plagiarism, copyright infringement, and trademark dilution". TechCrunch reported that "Just 10 of the 719 manuscripts included releases of the model's chain of thought" and that the advisory group's request for machine-readable metadata correlating the natural language and formal artifacts was "something that the frontier lab did not do with these releases". The statement carries no signatory count and records no OpenAI response.

The week's other mathematical results put the proof assistant first. Science issued "Advancing mathematics research with AI-driven formal proof search" by George Tsoukalas and 20 co-authors, volume 394 issue 6820 pages 234-239, reporting an agent that "autonomously resolved nine of 353 open Erdős problems, proved 44/492 On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences conjectures", and that "Even a basic agent alternating LLM-based generation with Lean-based verification replicated the Erdős successes." SqueezeBench, from TU Wien, checks every submitted record with "two independent Lean kernels, so no referee needs to check the mathematics", and reports frontier-model agents improving every one of its twenty initial records with 82 accepted submissions, while noting that "For eight of the ten problems, at least one record is still asymptotically behind the best published bound." A separate preprint, arXiv:2610.08144, reported that the Lean proof of OpenAI's announced Navier-Stokes blow-up "does not correspond to the NL proof", while stating: "We do not make claims about the correctness of OpenAI's NL proof, we only make statements about mistranslations into Lean." No lab has published an adoption statement for the advisory group's norms.
states.changed: The dispute moved from methodology to withdrawal and boycott: OpenAI retracted three manuscripts over a sign error, cut its catalogue to 719 manuscripts with 300 top-line results formalised, and a professional body urged mathematicians to stop working with the company. In the same days Science published a DeepMind agent whose deliverable is a machine-checked Lean proof, and a new benchmark made two independent Lean kernels the referee — so the week contained both halves of the argument about who does the checking.

text: As of 19 October the dispute has money behind the sceptics' side of it, supplied by the labs. The Simons Foundation announced "$15 million in combined funding and resources" with Anthropic and OpenAI, to be awarded including through an open call for proposals, for workshops and initiatives that help researchers evaluate recent AI-assisted results and shape collective standards for AI use; Anthropic and OpenAI are also to provide AI tools and computing resources, extending beyond mathematics to basic science. David Spergel framed it as community-led: "As artificial intelligence rapidly reshapes the research landscape, we want to help the mathematical community come together", and "The community should be driving discussions of how these tools are evaluated, adopted and used" — "not any single company or institution".

The checking question moved on the evidence side as well. A Lean-checked mathematics benchmark had frontier-model agents improve all 20 of its records, after which newer models improved 19 again, with two independent Lean kernels as the referee rather than a human reviewer or a lab's own write-up.

The arc's settling condition is still open. No lab has adopted the declaration's write-up norms, no joint statement has been issued, and the funding announcement names no programme title, no recipients and no governance for the money. The labs are paying for the assessment of their own results, and nothing published this week says who decides what gets assessed.
states.changed: The two labs at the centre of the dispute put money into the mathematicians' side of it: a combined $15 million with the Simons Foundation for work that helps researchers evaluate AI-assisted results and set standards for AI use, framed by the foundation as community-led rather than company-led. No write-up norms were adopted and no recipients, governance or programme name were published, so the arc's question is untouched.

text: As of 2 November the dispute has two claimants to the same result and the beginnings of outside scrutiny. The openai/math history file records two manuscripts added on October 26, each with a Lean formalization, one of them "The Exponential Time Hypothesis is False", described as a deterministic, subexponential-time, polynomial-space algorithm for exactly counting satisfying assignments of fixed-width CNF formulas, with the 3-SAT case refuting the hypothesis. Scientific American reports that "Mere hours after OpenAI's announcement, Anthropic posted its own independent result disproving ETH, based on work by an internal Anthropic model." OfficeChai says Anthropic's paper is titled "A 2^o(n) Time Algorithm for 3-SAT" with "Claude, Anthropic" as the listed author, and quotes its appendix saying the Lean development "was written by AI models and reviewed by other instances of the same models" and that "at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it".

The checking question the arc exists for is now live, with a qualification. Scientific American reports that Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego and Ryan Williams of MIT, who first suggested the hypothesis, "are now working with OpenAI to perform an independent investigation of the result", and that OpenAI "will also sponsor a computer science conference about the proof as part of this investigation, according to Williams". Lance Fortnow's Computational Complexity blog recorded that "Update (10/29): Impagliazzo, Paturi and Williams set up a site to discuss the ETH Refutation with a discussion blog and paper repository." Two papers reworking Anthropic's algorithm appeared on arXiv on 30 October without lab involvement: one gives a subquadratic integer 3SUM algorithm avoiding matrix multiplication and says it "disproves the k-SUM Hypothesis for all odd k", and the other makes the #3-SAT recursion explicit and lowers its crossover points.

Write-up norms are untouched, and the labs' own reporting still omits what the declaration asked for. Scientific American reports that "The large language model (LLM) that produced the new proofs remains proprietary, and the exact prompts used, time spent computing and 'chain of thought outputs' involved have not been made public", and says the releases "continue to contradict the recommendations of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI)". The OpenAI README still says unformalized results "could have issues", and its history file records three manuscripts withdrawn on October 7 after a sign error invalidated a stabilization-trace cancellation argument. On the verification side a preprint from Amazon Web Services and Case Western Reserve University reports a Lean system that "proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations" with an off-the-shelf frontier model and no additional training, while proving 1,054 of 2,000 statements, or 52.7%, on implementation-level obligations it built to replace the saturated benchmarks.
states.changed: Both labs now claim the same refutation. Anthropic posted its own Claude-authored disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis hours after OpenAI's, listing "Claude, Anthropic" as the author and stating in its appendix that the Lean development was reviewed only by other instances of the same models and that "at the time of writing no person is known to have checked it". The hypothesis's own authors have begun examining the OpenAI result — while OpenAI sponsors a conference about the proof — and the first papers reworking Anthropic's algorithm appeared on arXiv with no lab involvement. No write-up norms were adopted, and Scientific American reports the model, the prompts and the compute remain undisclosed.

text: As of 9 November the week's movement came from a company rather than from the mathematicians. TechCrunch reported that Axiom Math's agents translated the Stacks Project, the open-source algebraic geometry reference started by Columbia's Johan de Jong, into Lean code that a proof assistant checks line by line — about 7,654 pages of material turned into roughly 16 million lines of machine-checked code, announced on 4 November. Chief executive Carina Hong is quoted saying: "I openly challenge all the coding companies to work on formalization at this scale." Formal verification means a proof assistant has checked the steps, not that any result is new, and TechCrunch cites no independent audit of the library and says it found no primary post from Axiom describing the work.

Nothing in the week changed how the labs report mathematical results. No lab adopted the declaration's write-up norms, no joint statement appeared, and no development was reported on the Mathathon sponsorship. The figures above are Axiom's own as relayed by a single outlet. The arc's question — whether the dispute changes how labs report mathematical results, or how mathematicians engage with them — stands where it did, with the formalisation route now pushed by a venture-funded company rather than by the signatories.
states.changed: A new party entered the arc on the formalisation side: Axiom Math says its agents turned about 7,654 pages of the Stacks Project into roughly 16 million lines of Lean, and its chief executive publicly challenged coding companies to match it — a machine-checked route to the verifiability the declaration's signatories asked for, offered by a company rather than by a lab or by the mathematicians. Nothing moved on write-up norms, no lab responded, and no independent audit of the Lean library is cited.

questions.question: Will the Mathathon go ahead, and with whose sponsorship?
questions.would_settle: The organisers naming replacement sponsors or cancelling; the first round begins 30 October.

settled.text: It is going ahead without lab sponsorship. A joint statement set the redesigned event for 13 to 15 November 2026 under the theme "Old Problems, New Proofs", co-organised with the Foundation for Science and AI Research, with XTX Markets as lead donor.

questions.question: Will a lab claim be checked by an evaluator the lab did not select, pay or give review rights over the text?
questions.would_settle: A peer-reviewed publication by authors outside the lab, or a list of the resolved mathematics problems with citations.

questions.question: How many of OpenAI's 719 manuscripts are correct, and will anyone outside the company check the unformalised ones?
questions.would_settle: A peer-reviewed publication or journal referee report on one of the manuscripts, a further revision-log entry recording externally found errors, or a published count of formalisations by someone other than OpenAI.

questions.question: Will anyone outside the two labs certify either refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis?
questions.would_settle: A referee report, a published verification by mathematicians the labs did not select or pay, or a Lean artefact checked end to end by a named person and published with the kernel output.
